title: Gerunds and Infinitives in Everyday Life

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
One of the trickiest parts of English grammar is knowing when to use the <gerund> (-ing form) and when to use the <infinitive> (to + verb) after another verb. Native speakers use these patterns naturally, but for learners, it requires practice.

In this reading, we'll explore gerunds and infinitives through real-life situations — conversations, emails, and everyday decisions — so you can see how these patterns work in context.

sections.title: Situation 1: Planning a Weekend
sections.content:
Read this conversation between two friends:

Sarah: I <suggest> going to the Italian restaurant on Saturday.
Mark: I <enjoy> eating Italian food. But I <want> to go early — I <hate> waiting.
Sarah: I <agree> to meet at 7pm. Do you <fancy> watching a film after?
Mark: I'd <prefer> to go for a walk. I <need> to get more exercise.

Patterns: <suggest>, <enjoy>, <fancy> → <gerund> (-ing)
<want>, <agree>, <prefer>, <need> → <infinitive> (to + verb)

sections.title: Situation 2: A Work Email
sections.content:
Read this professional email:

Dear Team, I <hope> to share some updates. We <managed> to complete phase one on time. I <appreciate> everyone working so hard. I <suggest> scheduling a meeting this week. Please <avoid> booking Thursday.
I <look forward to> hearing your thoughts. — Lisa

Patterns: <hope>, <manage> → infinitive | <appreciate>, <suggest>, <avoid> → gerund | <look forward to> → gerund (to = preposition)

sections.title: Situation 3: Talking About Habits
sections.content:
Read how people describe their habits:

Tom: I <enjoy> running before work. I <can't stand> sitting all day.
Ana: I <love> cooking for my family. I <refuse> to eat fast food.
James: I <admit> spending too much time on my phone. I <plan> to read more.

Patterns: <refuse>, <plan> → infinitive | <enjoy>, <can't stand>, <admit> → gerund | <love> → both work

sections.title: Verbs That Change Meaning
sections.content:
Some verbs change meaning depending on gerund or infinitive:

<Remember>: I <remember> locking the door (= memory) vs I <remembered> to lock the door (= didn't forget)

<Stop>: She <stopped> smoking (= quit) vs She <stopped> to smoke (= paused to smoke)

<Try>: <Try> opening the window (= experiment) vs <Try> to open it (= make an effort)

<Forget>: I'll never <forget> meeting you (= memory) vs I <forgot> to meet you (= missed appointment)

sections.title: Summary
sections.content:
Key takeaways:

• <Gerund> verbs (enjoy, avoid, suggest, mind, keep, consider, admit) often describe reactions or ongoing situations.
• <Infinitive> verbs (want, decide, hope, plan, agree, refuse, manage) often express intentions or future actions.
• Some verbs (like, love, hate, start, prefer) accept <both> forms.
• After <prepositions> (interested in, good at, look forward to), always use gerund.
• A few verbs (remember, stop, try, forget) <change meaning> depending on the form.

learningObjectives: Recognize gerund and infinitive patterns in real-life contexts
Understand how these patterns appear in conversations and emails
Identify verbs that change meaning with gerund vs. infinitive
Apply gerund and infinitive rules to describe habits and plans
Distinguish between preposition + gerund and infinitive structures

keyVocabulary.definition: The -ing form of a verb used as a noun (e.g., swimming, reading)
The base form of a verb with 'to' (e.g., to swim, to read)
The grammatical structure that follows a verb
When a verb has different meanings with gerund vs. infinitive
keyVocabulary.example: Stop smoking (quit) vs. stop to smoke (pause)
